title: Easy exam 12
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: the single directory tree, filters in a pipeline, until, links, regular expressions against globs, the order of expansions, find depth, subshells and the session commands.

questions.title: One tree for all the disks
questions.text: How does Linux present several disks and partitions to the user?

options.t: They are all mounted on directories of one single tree that starts at `/`.
options.why: There are no drive letters: `/home` or `/mnt/usb` may be different partitions, but they look like ordinary directories.

options.t: Each disk or partition gets its own letter, such as `C:` or `D:`, with its own root.
options.why: That is the Windows model; in Linux there is only one root, `/`.

options.t: Each disk has its own tree, and `cd` switches between them.
options.why: `cd` only moves inside the one tree.

options.t: Only the first disk is visible; the others must be accessed through special device files.
options.why: Once mounted, a partition is used through its mount point like any directory.

questions.title: Counting distinct users
questions.text: Each line of `log` is a user name and a number, such as `ana 1`. Which statement about `cut -d' ' -f1 log | sort -u | wc -l` is FALSE?

options.t: `cut -d' ' -f1` keeps only the first field of every line, the user name.
options.why: True: `-d' '` sets the space as separator and `-f1` selects the first field.

options.t: `sort -u` sorts the names and drops the repeated ones.
options.why: True: `-u` keeps one copy of each.

options.t: The pipeline prints a single number.
options.why: True: that is what `wc -l` prints.

options.t: The number printed is the number of lines of `log`, repeated users included.
options.why: False: duplicates are removed by `sort -u` before `wc -l` counts, so it prints the number of different users.

questions.title: Looping until
questions.text: Which loop repeats its body as long as its condition is FALSE and stops when it becomes true?

options.t: `until`
options.why: `until cond; do ...; done` runs the body until the condition succeeds.

options.t: `while`
options.why: It repeats as long as the condition is true.

options.t: `for`
options.why: It repeats once for each word of a list.

options.t: `case`
options.why: It is not a loop: it chooses one branch by comparing a word with patterns.

questions.title: Permissions of a link
questions.text: `link` is a symbolic link to the regular file `file`. Which command shows the permissions of the link itself, not of `file`?

options.t: `ls -l link`
options.why: It shows `lrwxrwxrwx`: the first letter `l` says it is a symbolic link, and the link's own permissions are always `rwx` for everybody.

options.t: `ls -lL link`
options.why: `-L` follows the link, so it shows the permissions of `file`, such as `-rw-r--r--`.

options.t: `stat -L link`
options.why: `-L` makes `stat` follow the link and describe the file it points to.

options.t: `cat link`
options.why: It prints the content of `file`; it shows no permissions at all.

questions.title: Dot in grep and in ls
questions.text: The directory has the files `a.txt`, `axtxt` and `b.txt`. What does `ls | grep a.txt` print?

options.t: `a.txt` and `axtxt`
options.why: In a regular expression the dot matches any character, so `a.txt` matches `axtxt` as well.

options.t: Only `a.txt`
options.why: That would happen if the dot were an ordinary character, as it is in a shell glob.

options.t: `a.txt`, `axtxt` and `b.txt`
options.why: `b.txt` has no `a` in front of `txt`, so it does not match.

options.t: Nothing, because `grep` needs the option `-E` to use a dot as a wildcard.
options.why: The dot is part of the basic regular expressions that `grep` uses by default.

questions.title: The order of expansions
questions.text: In which order does bash apply these three steps to a typed command line?

options.t: Alias expansion, then variable expansion, then wildcard expansion.
options.why: Aliases are replaced first; then `$VAR` is expanded; the wildcards are expanded last, on the words that are left.

options.t: Wildcard expansion, then variable expansion, then alias expansion.
options.why: This is the reverse of the real order.

options.t: Variable expansion, then alias expansion, then wildcard expansion.
options.why: Aliases are looked at before the variables are expanded.

options.t: Wildcard expansion, then alias expansion, then variable expansion.
options.why: The wildcards are the last step of the three, not the first.

questions.title: Limiting the depth of find
questions.text: Which command lists only the `.txt` files that are directly inside `docs`, without entering its subdirectories?

options.t: `find docs -maxdepth 1 -name '*.txt'`
options.why: `-maxdepth 1` limits the search to the directory itself and its direct entries.

options.t: `find docs -mindepth 1 -name '*.txt'`
options.why: `-mindepth 1` only skips the starting point; it still goes into every subdirectory.

options.t: `find docs -maxdepth 0 -name '*.txt'`
options.why: Depth 0 is only `docs` itself, and its name does not end in `.txt`: nothing is printed.

options.t: `find docs -depth 1 -name '*.txt'`
options.why: `-depth` takes no number; `find` complains "paths must precede expression".

questions.title: A subshell and cd
questions.text: You are in `/home/ana`. What does `(cd /tmp; pwd); pwd` print?

options.t: `/tmp` and then `/home/ana`
options.why: The parentheses run the commands in a subshell, so its `cd` does not change the directory of the original shell.

options.t: `/tmp` twice
options.why: That would happen with `{ cd /tmp; pwd; }; pwd`, which runs in the same shell.

options.t: `/home/ana` twice
options.why: The first `pwd` runs after the `cd`, inside the subshell, so it prints `/tmp`.

options.t: `/tmp` and then an error, because `cd` cannot be used in parentheses.
options.why: `cd` works in a subshell; its effect just ends with the subshell.

questions.title: The most frequent words
questions.text: `words` has one word per line. Which statement about `sort words | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -3` is TRUE?

options.t: It prints the three most frequent words, each preceded by its count.
options.why: `uniq -c` counts equal adjacent lines (so the input is sorted first), `sort -nr` puts the biggest counts first and `head -3` keeps three lines.

options.t: It prints the first three words of the file in alphabetical order.
options.why: The counts and the second `sort` change the order and the content of the lines.

options.t: It prints three different words, without counts.
options.why: `uniq -c` adds the count at the start of every line.

options.t: It fails, because `sort` cannot appear twice in the same pipeline.
options.why: A command can be used as many times as needed.

questions.title: Who is logged in
questions.text: Which statement about the session commands is FALSE?

options.t: `whoami` prints the name of the user running the shell.
options.why: True.

options.t: `id` shows the UID, the GID and the groups of the user.
options.why: True.

options.t: `who` lists the users that are logged in at the moment.
options.why: True: with their terminals and login times.

options.t: `last` shows what each user is running right now.
options.why: False: `last` shows the history of past logins (from `/var/log/wtmp`). The current activity of each user is shown by `w`.
